summary: Brazil admits citizens of the EU, the UK and most of Latin America visa-free for up to 90 days, has required an eVisa (about USD 80.90) from US, Canadian and Australian citizens since 10 April 2025, and asks the remaining nationalities to apply at a Brazilian consulate.

fee.notes: Total including the service fee. Currently required from US, Canadian and Australian citizens; issued with up to 10 years' validity for US citizens and typically 5 years for Canadians and Australians.
Fees vary by nationality under Brazil's reciprocity rules — confirm the exact amount with the consulate where you apply.
The same VIVIS category covers business meetings, conferences and journalism; no paid work in Brazil is permitted. Fees vary by nationality; eVisa-eligible nationalities apply online instead.

passportValidity.text: Brazil requires your passport to be valid for the duration of your stay; at least 6 months' validity is recommended and is required for eVisa applications.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: Not an entry requirement for arrivals from most countries, but vaccination is strongly recommended for travel to the Amazon, the Pantanal, Iguaçu Falls and most inland states — and several onward countries require proof of vaccination from travellers who have been in Brazil.

source.name: Ministério da Saúde — Ministry of Health of Brazil

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance is not an entry requirement. Brazil's public SUS system treats emergencies free of charge, but private care — the practical option for visitors — must be paid for, so cover is recommended.

onwardTicket.text: Federal Police officers and airlines may ask visa-free and eVisa travellers for proof of return or onward travel within the permitted stay.

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is set, but officers may ask you to show means to support yourself during your stay, along with accommodation details.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of more than BRL 10,000 (or equivalent in any currency) must be declared electronically (e-DBV) on entry and exit; undeclared amounts above the limit can be seized.

notes: Goods worth up to USD 1,000 may be brought in duty-free by air (plus airport duty-free purchases).
Drones must generally be registered with ANATEL/ANAC before use in Brazil.

payments.text: Cards are accepted almost everywhere in cities and resorts, and the instant-payment system Pix dominates daily life — but Pix normally needs a Brazilian bank account, so visitors rely on cards plus some cash for beach vendors, markets and small towns.

safety.text: Violent and street crime are real risks in Brazilian cities: keep phones and jewellery out of sight, use app taxis at night, avoid deserted areas and beaches after dark, and never enter favelas without an organised, locally-vetted guide.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Brazil Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: The ideal season depends on the region: April–September is drier for the Amazon, the Pantanal and the northeast beaches, while December–March brings summer heat, rain — and Carnival — to Rio and the south.

tips.text: Apply for the Brazilian eVisa only through the official portal brazil.vfsevisa.com (linked from gov.br) — unofficial sites charge heavy mark-ups and some are scams.
Phone snatching is the most common crime against tourists — keep your phone off the street, carry a decoy wallet, and use ride-hailing apps instead of hailing cabs at night.

Brazil has no single voltage: sockets are 127 V in most tourist cities (Rio, São Paulo) but 220 V in many states, including Brasília and much of the northeast. Check the outlet label before plugging in.
Pix QR payments are ubiquitous but normally require a Brazilian bank account — carry a contactless card and small cash as a visitor.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Brazil?
faq.answer: Yes. Since 10 April 2025, US citizens need an eVisa to visit Brazil. It costs about USD 80.90, is applied for online at brazil.vfsevisa.com, and for US citizens is issued with up to 10 years' validity, allowing stays of up to 90 days per visit and 180 days per year.

faq.question: Which nationalities can visit Brazil without a visa?
faq.answer: Citizens of the EU, the UK, Switzerland, Japan, South Korea, Turkey, South Africa, Mexico and most of South America (among others) can visit visa-free for up to 90 days. US, Canadian and Australian citizens need the eVisa, and nationalities such as Chinese, Indian and Nigerian citizens need a consular visa.

faq.question: How do I apply for the Brazilian eVisa?
faq.answer: Apply online at the official portal brazil.vfsevisa.com with a passport photo page scan, a recent photo, proof of onward travel and funds, and pay about USD 80.90 by card. Processing is typically around 5 business days, but allow at least two weeks before travel.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever vaccination for Brazil?
faq.answer: It is not an entry requirement when arriving from most countries, but vaccination is strongly recommended for the Amazon, the Pantanal, Iguaçu Falls and most inland states — and some countries you travel to afterwards will demand the certificate because you have been in Brazil.

faq.question: Can I extend my 90-day stay in Brazil?
faq.answer: Most visa-free and eVisa visitors can apply to the Federal Police (Polícia Federal) before their first 90 days expire for one extension of up to 90 days, within an overall cap of 180 days in any 12-month period. Some nationalities (for example Germans and Italians) are capped at 90 days per 180-day period.
